idiom_name: static stored type property + instance computed property
implementation_notes: Swift's type properties are the pattern's static storage: a static stored property exists once per type, is lazily initialized on first access, and the Swift runtime guarantees the initialization runs only once even when several threads touch it first; instances of a struct stay ordinary value-semantics values that carry no data, so writing through one instance is visible through every other. What replaces the classic structure is the type property plus value-type instances: there is no static class to declare, and var current: Int { get { Self.level } set { Self.level = newValue } } is the idiomatic forwarding shape. Mutating a static stored property after initialization is not synchronized, and Swift 6 concurrency checking diagnoses it as unsafe shared mutable state - use the Mutex variant there.
pitfalls: Swift 6 reports a mutable static property as not concurrency-safe (nonisolated shared mutable state); by then the classic form needs a Mutex, a global actor, or nonisolated(unsafe).
Because instances are structs, copying one does not copy the state: let b = a produces an independent value that still reads and writes the same static slot.
Stored type properties cannot be overridden (only class computed ones can), so a subclass shares the same slot and cannot get its own copy.
Two copies of a dynamically loaded framework, or an extension compiled into another module, can end up with separate type metadata and therefore separate state.

variants.name: Mutex-guarded static state (Swift 6 concurrency-safe)
variants.implementation_notes: Under Swift 6 strict concurrency a mutable static property must either be isolated (a global actor such as @MainActor) or protected by a lock, so the concurrency-safe monostate stores the state in a static let Mutex value from the Synchronization module and exposes it through withLock from a computed property; instances keep value semantics and all reads and writes serialize on the one lock. Use this variant when the monostate is touched from more than one concurrency domain, @MainActor isolation when the state is UI-facing, and nonisolated(unsafe) only when an external lock already guards every access.
pitfalls: Mutex comes from the Synchronization module and needs Swift 6 plus a deployment target that supports it; older toolchains must fall back to OSAllocatedUnfairLock or a global actor.
withLock serializes access but the slot is still process-global, and Mutex is not reentrant - never call back into code that re-enters withLock.
nonisolated(unsafe) silences the diagnostic without adding synchronization; only use it when an external lock or dispatch queue really protects every access.
